statement: If a number have its half odd, it is even-times odd only.
heath_proof: For let the number A have its half odd; I say that A is even-times odd only. Now that it is even-times odd is manifest; for the half of it, being odd, measures it an even number of times. [VII. Def. 9] I say next that it is also even-times odd only. For, if A is even-times even also, it will be measured by an even number according to an even number; [VII. Def. 8] so that the half of it will also be measured by an even number though it is odd: which is absurd. Therefore A is even-times odd only.

9.33
**Statement:** If a number have its half odd, it is even-times odd only.

**Step 1.** Let A be a number whose half is odd, and let E be that half; so A = E + E, and E is odd. We must show that A is even-times odd, and that A is not even-times even.

**Step 2.** The dyad is an even number, for it is divisible into two equal parts, namely its two units [D7.6].

**Step 3.** Since A = E + E, A is E added to itself twice, that is, as many times as there are units in the dyad; hence E multiplied by the dyad makes A [D7.15]. Therefore the dyad multiplied by E also makes A [7.16]; that is, A is the dyad added to itself as many times as there are units in E, so that the dyad measures A according to the units in E [D7.15].

**Step 4.** Thus A is measured by an even number, the dyad (Step 2), according to an odd number, E (Step 1). Therefore A is even-times odd [D7.9].

**Step 5.** I say next that A is not also even-times even. For suppose, if possible, that it is. Then A is measured by some even number B according to some even number C [D7.8]; that is, A is the number made by adding B to itself as many times as there are units in C, namely B multiplied by C [D7.15].

**Step 6.** Since C is even, it is divisible into two equal parts [D7.6]; let F be its half, so that C = F + F. To add B to itself C times is to add B to itself F times and then F times again. Hence, if G is the number made by adding B to itself F times, that is, B multiplied by F [D7.15], we have A = G + G.

**Step 7.** But also A = E + E (Step 1). Therefore G = E. For if G were greater than E, exceeding it by some number K, then G + G would be E + E together with K + K, that is, A together with K + K; so A, which is G + G, would be equal to a number of which A is a part, whereas the whole is greater than the part [CN5], which is impossible. In the same way G cannot be less than E. Hence G = E.

**Step 8.** Therefore E, being equal to G, is B added to itself as many times as there are units in F (Step 6). Since B is even, E is either B itself (if F is an unit) or a sum of even numbers each equal to B; in either case E is even [9.21].

**Step 9.** But E is odd (Step 1). Thus E is at once divisible into two equal parts, being even [D7.6], and not so divisible, being odd [D7.7], which is absurd. Therefore A is not even-times even.

**Step 10.** Hence A is even-times odd (Step 4) and is not even-times even (Step 9); that is, A is even-times odd only. Q.E.D.
